title: Matthew 19:13–15
context: Right after the hard word on marriage and kingdom celibacy, parents bring children for Jesus’ hands and prayer. The disciples push them back; Jesus welcomes the little ones and names them as kingdom people.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about right after the hard word on marriage and kingdom celibacy, parents bring children for Jesus’ hands and prayer.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: That he should lay his hands on them - This was a rite which was very early used, in praying for a blessing on young persons. The disciples rebuked them - That is, them that brought them: probably thinking such an employ beneath the dignity of their Master.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 19:13–15)

reformed.quote: If a crown had been put on his head, they would have admitted it willingly, and with approbation; for they did not yet comprehend his actual office. But they reckon it unworthy of his character to receive children; and their error wanted not plausibility; for what has the highest Prophet and the Son of God to do with infants?
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 19:13–15)

verses.text: Then little children were brought to him that he should lay his hands on them and pray; and the disciples rebuked them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Parents seek Jesus’ touch and prayer for their children—a simple act of trust. The disciples, still sorting status and cost (vv. 10–12), rebuke the bringers as if little ones waste the Teacher’s time.

Grace still draws the overlooked to Jesus. Gatekeepers in the church can hinder what the Lord means to bless; hearers remain responsible not to scold away those who come in need of His hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew pairs blessing sought with disciples’ rebuke. Even close followers misread who belongs near the King.

Christ will correct His own. The church’s instincts about “important” ministry often exclude the weak until the Lord reorders the circle.

verses.text: But Jesus said, “Allow the little children, and don’t forbid them to come to me; for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus’ double command—let them come; do not hinder—opens the way and forbids obstruction. To such belongs the kingdom echoes 18:3–4: childlike dependence, not achievement, marks kingdom people.

The invitation is sincere. Grace brings children (and the childlike) to Christ; adults must not block that approach. The kingdom is gift received, not prize earned by the impressive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Authority speaks: come, and stop hindering. Kingdom membership is assigned to such—the lowly and dependent—not to the self-important.

Christ defines belonging. The same Lord who builds His church welcomes little ones as rightful heirs of heaven’s reign, exposing pride that treats them as interruption.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear a welcome and a serious warning against hindering. Arminians typically emphasize the open summons grace enables parents and children to answer; Calvinists stress that kingdom belonging is Christ’s to grant—displayed here in the little ones He claims—rather than a status disciples may police.

verses.text: He laid his hands on them, and departed from there.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus does what was asked: He lays hands on them. The scene ends not with a lecture to the children but with His blessing enacted, then departure.

Grace that welcomes also touches. Ministry to the young is not sentimental add-on; it is following the Lord who stops for them before He moves on.
verses.reformedNotes:
Word and gesture agree. Hands confirm the verbal welcome; then He proceeds on His appointed way.

Christ’s blessing is concrete. The church that knows its King will neither romanticize childhood nor despise it—receiving little ones because He first received them.
